name: Sericin hydrogel dressing

card.summary: A moist wound dressing or skin mask made from sericin, the silk protein from silkworm cocoons, used to keep skin hydrated and support healing so skin and scars look better.
card.aka: silk sericin gel, silk protein hydrogel, sericin mask
card.note: Silk-protein products can cause reactions in people with silk allergy; medical wound dressings are used under clinical guidance.

quick.overview:
Sericin is the sticky protein that holds silk fibres together in a silkworm cocoon. Made into a water-rich gel or sheet, it is used as a wound dressing and as an ingredient in hydrating skincare masks.

The appearance payoff is through skin condition: holding moisture against the skin and supporting wound repair can leave skin smoother and recovering wounds looking better. Research includes randomised trials in burn wounds and cosmetic studies of skin-ageing measures, mostly small and on sericin-containing formulas rather than plain hydrogel sheets.
quick.how: Sericin appears in moisturisers, serums and sheet masks, and in medical dressings, sometimes combined with other materials such as bacterial cellulose. Users apply it to the skin like any hydrating product; wound dressings are applied in clinical settings.
quick.risks: Sericin is generally described as biocompatible, but early silk sutures with residual sericin were linked to biocompatibility problems, which is why medical silk is usually processed to remove it. People allergic to silk should be cautious, and wounds that are not healing need medical review.

lead: Sericin is a protein produced by the silkworm Bombyx mori that forms the glue-like coating on silk fibres. It makes up roughly 20 to 30 percent of raw silk, with the rest being fibroin [1]. Extracted from cocoons, it can be formed into gels, films and hydrogels, which are water-rich materials used as wound dressings and cosmetic masks [2][3].

For appearance, the interest is in skin hydration and repair. Wikipedia reports that sericin gels have been described as improving skin elasticity and reducing water loss, and reviews describe its biocompatibility and hydrophilicity [1][2]. Randomised trials have tested sericin in burn wounds, in a wound dressing combining it with bacterial cellulose, and in a skin-ageing complex [4][5][6].

chain: Sericin gel or dressing keeps skin moist
angle.text: Sericin gels and masks are applied to hydrate skin, and sericin dressings are used on wounds to support healing. Skin that is better hydrated and wounds that heal cleanly can look better.

paras: Sericin is rich in serine, which gives it its adhesive, hydrating character, and its structure shifts between random coil and beta-sheet depending on moisture and stretch [1]. Reviews list properties including biocompatibility, biodegradability, non-toxicity and hydrophilicity, and its ability to form gels, nanoparticles and films [2][3].

In skincare, sericin appears in moisturisers and serums, and a controlled study compared hydrating effects of hyaluronic acid, sericin, glycerol and urea in two vehicles on the forearms of 20 volunteers [7]. A split-face randomised study tested a complex of gold silk sericin, niacinamide and another ingredient on skin-ageing measures [5].

In medicine, sericin is incorporated in dressings. A bacterial cellulose dressing containing sericin and polyhexamethylene biguanide was tested in a randomised trial for wound treatment [6], and a randomised trial examined sericin in burn wounds [4]. Reviews describe sericin in tissue engineering and drug delivery [3][8].

Randomised trials include one on silk sericin in burn wound healing [4], a split-face study of a sericin complex on skin ageing [5], a trial of a sericin and PHMB bacterial-cellulose dressing [6], and a placebo-controlled trial in which sericin cream was used for itching in hemodialysis patients [9]. These test specific formulations, and most are small.

A review of silk biomaterials notes that biocompatibility problems reported with older silk sutures were likely caused by residual sericin, and that purified silk fibroin showed biocompatibility comparable to other common materials [10]. Sericin extracted and processed for modern products is described as biocompatible in reviews [2].
